title: IDC6940 Bayesian Housing Prices

Lucas Alderfer and Hunter Evans


Abstract


Introduction
Introduction DRAFT
This analysis is a statistical extension to this paper: [Paper reference]. The overall goal of this paper was to see how much evacuation zones, along with other socioeconomic variables, were affecting the prices of homes. The statistical techniques used in the paper were OLS with spatial error model (SEM) along with Difference in Differences (DID). Our extension to model it as a Hierarchical Bayesian Spatial Error Model (HBSEM) which integrates three distinct statistical modeling frameworks: hierarchical structure, Bayesian inference, and spatial autoregression.
The Hierarchical structure uses nested structures to allow for varying slopes based on different predictors. This allows for more accurate predictions based on the variable of your choosing. . As Gałecki and Burzykowski (2013) note, mixed-effects models allow researchers to “model both the mean structure and the variance-covariance structure of the response variable” while accommodating data where “observations are grouped or clustered”. This will allow us to vary the slopes of our evacuation groups allowing for a more accurate picture of how it affects the prices.
The Bayesian framework replaces fixed point estimation with full posterior probability distributions for every parameter, conditional on observed data and specified prior distributions. As Johnson et al. (2022) explain, Bayesian methods excel because they “provide a natural framework for updating our understanding of the world as new evidence becomes available, fully capturing parameter uncertainty through posterior distributions rather than relying on asymptotic p-values”.
Home costs naturally violate the classical assumption of independent and identically distributed errors due to shared locational amenities, coastal proximity, and unobserved neighborhood externalities. As Anselin (1988) highlights in his foundational text, “The spatial dimension in economic data implies that observations located in close proximity are dependent, requiring explicit modeling of the spatial error structure to avoid biased standard errors and spurious inferences”. By embedding a Conditional Autoregressive (CAR) prior over the spatial error process, our HBSEM model absorbs latent spatial spillovers allowing for these proximity errors to not affect our estimates.
By combining these three components, our approach provides a robust framework for isolating localized flood risk penalties from spatial noise. The remainder of this report details the work we did fitting the data, checking assumptions, and concluding.


Exploratory research included a literature review of various statistical methods used in econometric analysis, instructional texts for Bayesian and Spatial analyses and their overlap, and approaches to large datasets. This led us to using our CAR and hierarchical subsumption of an SEM model to approach the data.
Assessing housing prices in areas that are vulnerable to environmental risks has incessantly demanded statistical methods with the capability to account for spatial dependences, hierarchical structures, and accurate uncertainty measures. Regression models have provided a sufficient foundation for estimating the relationship between building characteristics and housing prices, though geographically referenced data violates our assumptions of independence. This becomes pertinent when evaluating markets among coastal regions, whereas nearby properties typically share environmental, economic, and geodemographic characteristics. The literature reviewed for this extension spans structural equation modeling (SEM), hierarchical and mixed-effects models, spatial econometrics, Bayesian methods, and empirical studies of housing markets influenced by storms and environmental occurrences. The collective reviews have motivated the use of a hierarchical conditional autoregressive (CAR) subsumption of an SEM framework for analyzing housing prices.
SEM (if we are using) Structural equation modeling allows for a broader statistical analysis for examining relationships among multiple variables concurrently. Anderson and Gerbing (1988) established the SEM two-step approach wherein the measurement model is evaluated and subsequently the structural relationships among variables are estimated. This allows for a better distinction between the representation of constructs and the relationships among constructs. The present study focuses on observed housing and geographic variables, and an extension using the SEM framework provides an opportunity to represent multiple interconnected relationships within the model.
An important consideration in SEM is the potential effect of model misspecification, or where the model proposed does not accurately align with the true data-generating process. Curran et al. (2002) examines the behavior of the noncentral chi-square distribution under misspecified structural equation modeling using Monte Carlo simulations. They demonstrated that model fit and inference can be affected by the degree and type of misspecification in finite samples. This is a concern when approaching housing data as observations may be correlated because of geographical clustering or unaccounted path influences. As such, treating observations as independent when a spatial of hierarchical dependence is present could result in an incorrectly specific model. Extending to an SEM framework allows for the explicit account of spatial and hierarchical dependencies and addressing a potential source of misspecification.
Hierarchy and mixed effects Housing data naturally possesses hierarchical characteristics due to the grouping of properties within municipalities, evacuation zones, and other geographic units. Therein observations within the groups may contain characteristics that are not entirely captured by the measured predictors. Galecki and Burzykowski (2013) provide a framework for linear mixed-effects models that emphasizes the distinction between fixed and random effects while demonstrating the incorporation of hierarchical structures into regression models. Treatments include random intercepts and random slopes that allows for relationships to vary across groups rather than assuming that a singular coefficient applies identically to all observations.
The present study requires this consideration as housing prices and characteristics may vary geographically and is likely not constant across all locations and housing price brackets. A hierarchical integration can accommodate for this variation by allowing parameters to differ across groups while still accessing information throughout said groups. This gives an alternative method to having to estimate separate models for each geographic location and allows for more efficient and robust estimations.
Spatial While the hierarchical integration will address potential clustering, spatial statistics will provide the more directed framework for managing geographic dependencies. Anselin (1988) established the foundational methods for spatial econometrics by highlighting spatial dependence and spatial heterogeneity. Spatial dependence occurs when observations in one geographic location are correlated with observations in nearby locations, while spatial heterogeneity is when relationships are differing across geographic spaces. Neighboring properties are unlikely to represent independent observations and as such the spatial characteristics are important to our assessments of housing markets.
Spatial econometrics models incorporate the geographic relationships through spatial weight matrices and related spatial processes. Spatial lag and error models provide a mechanism to incorporate dependencies among neighboring observations. As amenity proximity, environmental risks, and market conditions are not restricted to individual properties, evaluating housing prices with spatial concepts becomes exceptionally relevant. This is furthered by LeSage and Pace (2017) in their demonstrations. They show that coefficients in spatial models cannot always be interpreted in the same manner as coefficients from typical regression models. Spatial dependence can contribute direct and indirect effects, and as such a change in a single observation can bleed to neighboring observations through the spatial structure. Their approach with Monte Carlo simulations illustrates how evaluating spatial estimator behaviors becomes more important than relying entirely on conventional interpretations of coefficients. As the objective with the current study is to further account for the geographic structures in that housing market relationships are operating, we will be broadening the scope past identifying significant predictors of the market.

Readings
- Sahu (2024)
This book provides instruction on modeling Spatio-Temporal data using Bayesian methods in R. The section of interest is chapter 7 “Bayesian modeling for point referenced spatio-temporal data”. It outlines three stage hierarchical structure used by Bayesian spatio-temporal models. It discusses how continuous data is modeled using Gaussian models and how spatial and temporal aspects are captured with Gaussian processes and autoregressive models and seperable covariance structures. It goes through the nugget effect, a popular approach to seperating spatio-temporal dependence from independent measurement error. It aslo discusses why seperable models are better for computational efficiency while maintaining prediction accuracy.
- Wikle, Zammit-Mangion, and Cressie (2019)
This book is one of the main references for spatial statistics and has further development on the three hierarchical stages of a model. This is the observation model, the process model, and the parameter model. This lets us combine our observed data with our assumptions while accounting for uncertainty and implement Bayesian reasoning. With this methodology we can share information between time and location points and make better uncertainty estimates with our predictions.
- Galecki and Burzykowski (2013)
This text provides a practical, step-by-step guide to fitting linear mixed-effects (LME) models using R, primarily leveraging the nlme and lme4 packages. It systematically bridges classical linear regression with mixed-effects frameworks, focusing on model formulation, estimation methods (such as Maximum Likelihood and Restricted Maximum Likelihood), and diagnostics for complex data structures.
This book serves as a core reference for hierarchical and multilevel data modeling. It details how to handle nested, repeated-measures, and clustered structures by incorporating both fixed and random effects. Citing this text validates the foundational rules of hierarchical linear models, random intercepts, random slopes, and the explicit modeling of within-group variation.
- Anselin (1988)
Luc Anselin’s foundational text formally introduced spatial econometrics as a distinct field within regional science and quantitative geography. The book establishes the theoretical framework required to model spatial dependence (where observations in one location affect nearby locations) and spatial heterogeneity (where statistical relationships vary across space). It covers spatial autoregressive processes, diagnostic tests for spatial autocorrelation, and estimation techniques like Maximum Likelihood.This text provides the seminal spatial facts and methodological rules for geographically arranged data. Utilizing Anselin’s principles establishes fundamental concepts such as spatial weight matrices (\(W\)), spatial lag models, and spatial error models. These frameworks ensure spatial structure and spatial autocorrelation are properly accounted for rather than treated as simple independence violations.
- LeSage and Pace (2017)
LeSage’s article discusses the misrepresentations coefficients and can produce when assessing spatial models and address shortcomings of their previous research. They instead choose to approach economic data with a Monte Carlo method study and produce a demonstration about the issues of previous approaches and how Monte Carlo circumvents them. For their Monte Carlo instructional they include a branch of Bayesian approach. They conclude that more attention needs to have been brought to the direct and indirect effects estimates and further Monte Carlo practices should consider this for spatial models.
- Walls, Magliocca, and McConnell (2018)
This paper assesses a spatial simulation model of coastal real estate and addressing the influence of storms and amenities (rec access, aesthetics, views, etc). Their model is parameterized to eastern US regions that experience hurricanes at a low rate and then is evaluated to see how spatial patterns of development would change if the frequency of storms was increased. They found that significantly increasing the probability of a hurricane did not change the spatial patterns of development in a meaningful way. If their low hurricane region’s storm possibility was increased to match that of states facing the Gulf of Mexico and all else equal, they found that development continued over time. They found coastal amenities to impact location patterns more. These findings may be important when considering how our own model behaves as Pinellas county is in South Florida and heavily impacted by hurricanes.
- Morgan, Douthat, and Lin (2022)
This is the paper that we are basing our analysis on for the capstone. The goal is to take this paper’s data and add beefier statistical concepts. Our current ideas are Bayesian, hierarchical models, and maybe add a spatial component. This paper was written in 2022, and analyzed home prices given a multitude of different variables. The main focus of these being evacuation zone changes, and how it effected the home prices. Numerous other variables are in the model as well. The statistical concepts used were a basic OLS with a spatial error term and Difference in differences (DID). There were about 170,000 data points in the data they used, with the new data we have up to about 270,000. Results showed that a numerous of terms were significant from all areas including distance to shoreline, amenities, and race. The professor thinks that Bayesian can add to this analysis, and we further hypothesize allowing a term like evacuation zone to fluctuate with different slopes could strengthen our analysis.
- Johnson, Ott, and Dogucu (2022)
This is the Bayes Rules text book that we will be basing our Bayesian Analysis on. Dr. Seals used it in the Applied Bayesian course, and since we are all comfortable with the package and the theory in this textbook we are going to use it in the paper. This book goes through a basic framework of Bayesian starting from the ground up, explaining at a basic what Bayesian is, and how to apply it to more advanced data. The book built its own package in R called bayesrules, which makes the use of Bayesian and explanation that much simpler. To tie this into our paper, the goal is to add a Bayesian model to allow for prior knowledge to seep through and allow for better estimations. Since our data is so large and has so many predictors, we hope that Bayesian can add an extra element to strengthen the analysis.
- Chandra-Putra and Andrews (2020)
The article assesses real estate prices in two New Jersey towns after hurricane Sandy in 2012. They used an ABM computer simulation model to answer their research questions both about real estate prices in response to coastal flooding and to assess policies in place that may affect or be affected by these floods and aftermaths. They found that preemptive measures such as structural considerations and education had an impact on the amount of claims and fluctuations within the market. This article is helpful for our research because it suggests that spatial statistics may have a bigger impact on our project than originally included.
- Bin and Polasky (2004)
This article has a similar assessment but for a town in North Carolina after hurricane Floyd. They use a “property price function” that is a least squares regression model to assess similar factors rather than a simulation. They overall found a house that is located within a floodplain has a lower cost than a similar and comparable house that is not located in a floodplain. They also found that the discount for existing in the floodplain was higher after hurricane Floyd than before. This article helped see how people are using OLS to model this area of research and compare it to the one used within the article we are expanding on.
